summary: This proposed standard extends the Routing Information Protocol (RIP) so each route can carry additional information, and it updates RFC 1058. It was the first specification of what became RIP version 2. It was replaced by RFC 1723.

eli5.summary: Routers swap lists of places they can reach. This update lets each item on the list carry extra notes, so routers can share more useful details with each other.

questions: how does rip carry additional information
what is the rip multicast address
why does rip-2 need subnet masks
subtitle: An extension to RIP that lets each route carry additional information like subnet masks and autonomous system numbers.

tldr.problem: RIP is simple and widespread, but it lacks information that modern networks need: subnet masks, security, and the ability to label routes with their origin. RIP packets also have unused space that can be reused.
tldr.mechanism: RIP version 2 redefines unused fields in the RIP packet to carry a subnet mask for each route, a route tag for EGP/BGP integration, a next hop to optimize paths, and an authentication field. The version field in the header marks RIP-2 packets.
tldr.outcome: RIP-2 is backward compatible with RIP-1; RIP-1 routers can coexist with RIP-2 routers on the same network, though multicast can be used to exclude RIP-1 systems. RFC 1388 was replaced by RFC 1723 with the same functionality.

today: RFC 1388 was replaced by RFC 1723, which is the current standard for RIP version 2 and remains the specification used in deployments today.

sections.title: Why RIP Needs An Update
sections.content:
RIP has been popular for decades because it is simple and lightweight. But it predates CIDR (subnets), autonomous systems, and modern security. The RIP packet format contains a lot of unused space that was reserved for future use. RIP-2 defines what goes in those spaces without changing the basic protocol structure.

RIP will remain useful in small networks where its simplicity is an advantage and where the overhead of OSPF or IS-IS is not justified. RIP-1 is still in wide deployment. RIP-2 lets these networks gain important new capabilities without abandoning their routing protocol.
sections.eli5: RIP is old and simple, but networks have grown and need more features. RIP-2 adds those features without breaking old RIP routers.

sections.title: The RIP-2 Packet Format
sections.content:
A RIP packet contains command and version bytes followed by a routing domain number. After that come route entries. In RIP-1, each entry has an address family, an IP address, and a metric. RIP-2 redefines two unused fields: one becomes the subnet mask for the route, another becomes the next hop address.

All fields are in big-endian (network) byte order. The version field distinguishes RIP-2 from RIP-1. A router receiving a RIP-2 packet with an unknown version field should not discard it; this forward compatibility lets future RIP versions work with older implementations.
sections.eli5: The packet structure is the same shape as RIP-1, but some empty spots now mean subnet mask and where to forward packets.

sections.title: Authentication and Routing Domains
sections.content:
RIP-2 adds a way to authenticate route updates. If the first entry in the packet has an address family identifier of 0xFFFF, that entry is not a route; it is an authentication entry containing a 16-byte password (the "simple password" authentication type). The rest of the packet contains up to 24 regular route entries.

The Routing Domain field lets a single network segment run multiple independent RIP clouds. A router can filter updates by routing domain, supporting policy and network segmentation. The default routing domain is 0.
sections.eli5: RIP-2 can password-protect route updates. It can also run multiple separate RIP networks on the same wire.

sections.title: Route Tags and Next Hop
sections.content:
The Route Tag field is reserved for use with Exterior Gateway Protocols like EGP and BGP. It carries the autonomous system number of the route's origin. Any RIP system receiving a route with a non-zero tag must re-advertise that tag unchanged. Routes learned locally that have no external origin get a tag of zero.

The Next Hop field specifies which neighbor to forward packets to instead of the router sending the advertisement. This optimizes paths when RIP is not running on all routers on a network. If the Next Hop is 0.0.0.0, packets go to the advertiser. The field is advisory: ignoring it produces a valid but possibly sub-optimal path.
sections.eli5: The route tag remembers where the route came from (which autonomous system). The next hop field says who to give packets to, to avoid extra hops.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility with RIP-1
sections.content:
RIP-1 routers ignore version 2 packets with non-zero values in fields marked "Must Be Zero" (MBZ). But RFC 1058 wisely said implementations should not discard packets of version greater than 1 just because MBZ fields are non-zero. This forward-compatibility rule means RIP-1 systems can coexist with RIP-2 systems on the same segment.

A compatibility switch in implementations controls whether to send RIP-1 packets, RIP-2 packets with broadcasting (for RIP-1 compatibility), or RIP-2 packets with multicasting (for RIP-2 only). The multicast address is 224.0.0.9. RIP-1 will not receive multicast messages, so using multicast effectively isolates RIP-2 networks if desired.
sections.eli5: Old RIP routers can ignore the new RIP-2 fields and still work. Networks can choose to send only to RIP-2 routers using multicast, or to send to both old and new routers using broadcast.

fields.name: Route Tag
fields.desc: Autonomous system number for EGP/BGP routes.

fields.name: Subnet Mask
fields.desc: The subnet mask for the route; zero if not included.

fields.name: Next Hop
fields.desc: IP address to forward to; 0.0.0.0 means the advertiser.
